claim: The Drosophila mushroom body (MB) is required for the acquisition and recall of associative olfactory memories.
source: It has been demonstrated that the MB is required for the acquisition and recall of associative olfactory memories (de Belle and Heisenberg, 1994)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to de Belle and Heisenberg, 1994.

claim: Projection neurons (PNs) are connected in a largely stochastic manner to approximately 2000 Kenyon cells (KCs) per brain hemisphere.
source: PNs are connected in a largely stochastic manner to the approximately 2000 KCs per brain hemisphere, resulting in a unique KC odor representation in individual flies (Litwin-Kumar et al., 2017; Aso et al., 2014a; Caron et al., 2013; Gruntman and Turner, 2013; Lin et al., 2007; Betkiewicz et al., 2020; Eichler et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: A population of food-responsive PNs shows partial non-random connectivity, which is an exception to the largely stochastic connectivity pattern.
source: The exception to this is a partial non-random connectivity of a population of food-responsive PNs (Zheng et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zheng et al., 2022.

claim: Any given odor activates approximately 3–9% of Kenyon cells.
source: Electrophysiological and calcium imaging studies demonstrated that any given odor activates approximately 3–9% of KCs (Campbell et al., 2013; Honegger et al., 2011; Turner et al., 2008; Siegenthaler et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to electrophysiological and calcium imaging studies.

claim: Mushroom body output neurons (MBONs) subdivide the MB lobes into distinct structural and functional modules by virtue of their dendritic arborizations.
source: KCs then transmit this odor information to mushroom body output neurons (MBONs) that subdivide the MB lobes into distinct structural and functional modules by virtue of their dendritic arborizations (Owald et al., 2015a; Aso et al., 2014b; Hige et al., 2015a; Cognigni et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Dopaminergic neurons (DANs) of the PPL1 cluster preferentially provide input to the vertical lobe of the MB and are activated during negative reinforcement.
source: DANs of the PPL1 cluster preferentially provide input to the vertical lobe of the MB and are activated during negative reinforcement, while DANs of the PAM cluster are activated during positive reinforcement and modulate activity in the horizontal lobe of the MB (Handler et al., 2019; Aso and Rubin, 2016; Tomchik and Davis, 2009; Séjourné et al., 2011; Cohn et al., 2015; Burke et al., 2012; Rohwedder et al., 2016; Saumweber et al., 2018; Selcho et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: DANs of the PAM cluster are activated during positive reinforcement and modulate activity in the horizontal lobe of the MB.
source: DANs of the PPL1 cluster preferentially provide input to the vertical lobe of the MB and are activated during negative reinforcement, while DANs of the PAM cluster are activated during positive reinforcement and modulate activity in the horizontal lobe of the MB (Handler et al., 2019; Aso and Rubin, 2016; Tomchik and Davis, 2009; Séjourné et al., 2011; Cohn et al., 2015; Burke et al., 2012; Rohwedder et al., 2016; Saumweber et al., 2018; Selcho et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The majority of MBONs of the vertical lobe utilize acetylcholine as a neurotransmitter and artificial activation of these MBONs often mediates approach behavior.
source: The majority of MBONs of the vertical lobe utilize acetylcholine as a neurotransmitter, and artificial activation of these MBONs often mediates approach behavior (Aso et al., 2014b; Eschbach et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Aso et al., 2014b and Eschbach et al., 2021.

claim: The majority of MBONs of the horizontal lobe release glutamate as a neurotransmitter and these neurons mediate avoidance behavior.
source: In contrast, the majority of MBONs of the horizontal lobe release glutamate as a neurotransmitter, and these neurons mediate avoidance behavior (Aso et al., 2014b; Eschbach et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Aso et al., 2014b and Eschbach et al., 2021.

claim: The activity of individual MBONs can be altered by conditioning paradigms.
source: In vivo calcium imaging and electrophysiological experiments demonstrated that the activity of individual MBONs can be altered by conditioning paradigms (Hige et al., 2015a; Aso and Rubin, 2016; Plaçais et al., 2013; Owald et al., 2015a; Jacob and Waddell, 2020; Perisse et al., 2016; Felsenberg et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to in vivo calcium imaging and electrophysiological experiments.

claim: Modulation of MBON activity depends on the pairing of DAN and KC activity and results in either an enhancement or depression of the strength of the KC>MBON connection.
source: This modulation of MBON activity depends on the pairing of DAN and KC activity and results in either an enhancement or depression of the strength of the KC>MBON connection (Handler et al., 2019; Owald et al., 2015a; Cohn et al., 2015; Burke et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Modulation of a relatively small number of KCs is sufficient to significantly alter memory recall.
source: These studies indicate that modulation of a relatively small number of KCs is sufficient to significantly alter memory recall.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from genetic tagging studies mentioned in the preceding sentence.

claim: MBON-α3 is an MBON at the tip of the α-lobe that is relevant for long-term memory.
source: We focus on MBON-α3 (MBON-14 in the terminology of Aso et al., 2014a), an MBON at the tip of the α-lobe that is relevant for long-term memory (Aso et al., 2014b; Plaçais et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Aso et al., 2014b and Plaçais et al., 2013.

claim: The resting membrane potential of MBON-α3 is in line with prior measurements of MBONs in vivo and of other central neurons in Drosophila.
source: This value for the resting membrane potential is in line with prior measurements of MBONs in vivo and of other central neurons in Drosophila (Hige et al., 2015a; Wilson et al., 2004; Gu and O'Dowd, 2006; Groschner et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with cited literature.

claim: MBON-α3 is highly excitable, with small input currents being sufficient to significantly alter its membrane potential.
source: MBON-α3 is thus highly excitable, with small input currents being sufficient to significantly alter its membrane potential.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the high membrane resistance measurement.

claim: The small amplitudes of action potentials in MBON-α3 are likely a result of the unipolar morphology of the neuron with a long neurite connecting the dendritic input region to the soma.
source: The small amplitudes are likely a result of the unipolar morphology of the neuron with a long neurite connecting the dendritic input region to the soma (see below).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the neuron's morphology and comparison with literature.

claim: Signal propagation in MBON-α3 may partially bypass the soma.
source: As a result, signal propagation may partially bypass the soma (Figure 1A, B and F; Gouwens and Wilson, 2009).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from morphology and supported by citation and figures.

claim: MBON-α3 is a spike-frequency adapting neuron.
source: This is consistent with the general idea that action potentials are "all or nothing" events, and that MBON-α3 is a spike-frequency adapting neuron constistent with prior observations of other MBONs (Hige et al., 2015a).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and comparison with cited literature.

claim: MBON-α3 receives 12,770 synaptic connections from 948 innervating Kenyon cells.
source: For our in silico model of MBON-α3, we used the recently published electron-microscopy-based connectome of the Drosophila mushroom body (Takemura et al., 2017). This dataset includes the precise morphological parameters of the entire dendritic tree including the precise location data for all 12,770 synaptic connections from the 948 innervating KCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the electron microscopy-based connectome.

claim: The EM-based reconstruction potentially misses 10% of synapses.
source: It is important to note that this dataset represents a single fly and the EM-based reconstruction was not able to faithfully assign all synaptic connections (potentially missing 10% of synapses; Takemura et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Takemura et al., 2017.

claim: The dendritic tree of MBON-α3 was subdivided into 4336 linear sections for the in silico model.
source: Based on the published vector data (Takemura et al., 2017) we subdivided the dendritic tree into 4336 linear sections, of which 3121 are postsynaptic to one or more of the 12,770 synaptic contacts from 948 KCs (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by the modeling methodology and reference to Figure 2B.

claim: 3121 dendritic sections of MBON-α3 are postsynaptic to one or more of the 12,770 synaptic contacts from 948 KCs.
source: Based on the published vector data (Takemura et al., 2017) we subdivided the dendritic tree into 4336 linear sections, of which 3121 are postsynaptic to one or more of the 12,770 synaptic contacts from 948 KCs (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by the modeling methodology and reference to Figure 2B.

claim: Linear cable theory is the baseline model for neurites and the most rational approach in the absence of detailed information about potential nonlinear currents.
source: We used linear cable theory (Niebur, 2008) to generate the in silico model of MBON-α3. Linear cable theory is the baseline model for neurites and the most rational approach in the absence of detailed information about potential nonlinear currents.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and citation.

claim: The average number of synaptic contacts from a KC to MBON-α3 is 13.47.
source: The average number of synaptic contacts from a KC to this MBON is 13.47 (Takemura et al., 2017), Figure 4B.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from Takemura et al., 2017 and Figure 4B.

claim: MBON-α3 is electrotonically compact.
source: These results indicate that the morphological architecture and biophysical parameters of MBON-α3 promote a 'compactification', or 'democratization', of synaptic inputs, with all inputs resulting in similar voltage excursions at the proximal neurite and soma, regardless of the strength of the initial dendritic voltage or the position on the dendritic tree.
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results showing similar voltage excursions across different input locations.

claim: The characteristic length (λ ≈ 1,300 μm) is about twice the maximal path length between any two segments of MBON-α3.
source: This is about twice the maximal path length between any two segments of the cell, see Figure 2C.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of the calculated characteristic length with the cell morphology shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The morphology of the MBON-α3 dendritic tree is finely tuned to maximize the equality of the functional weight of all synapses.
source: It is highly remarkable, however, that the morphology of the MBON-α3 dendritic tree seems finely tuned, with the goal of maximizing the equality of the functional weight of all synapses.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from simulation results showing compensation of voltage differences.

claim: The number of synapses per KC innervating MBON-α3 ranges from 1 to 27, with one outlier having 38 synaptic contacts.
source: The number of synapses varied between KCs, ranging from 1 to 27 (plus one outlier with 38 synaptic contacts), with a mean of 13.47 synapses per KC (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: MBON-α3 is in a small-signal operation mode, with a highly linear relation between the voltage excursion and the number of synapses per KC.
source: The neuron is firmly in a small-signal operation mode, as we observed a highly linear relation between the voltage excursion and the number of synapses per KC, Figure 4E.
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Activation of 13 randomly selected synapses in 1000 independent trials resulted in similar voltage excursions as observed for the KCs with 13 synaptic connections.
source: Activation of 13 randomly selected synapses in 1000 independent trials resulted in similar voltage excursions as observed for the KCs with 13 synaptic connections.
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results comparing random and anatomical synapse activation.

claim: In simulations with random synapse activation, the responses showed less variability compared to the activation of individual KCs with synapses at anatomically observed locations.
source: Interestingly, in these simulations the responses showed less variability compared to the activation of individual KCs with synapses at anatomically observed locations (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Activation of 50 KCs is sufficient to induce changes in the firing frequency of MBON-α3.
source: These results are consistent with an activation of 50 KCs being sufficient to induce changes in the firing frequency of MBON-α3 (Figure 1H, I).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from simulation results and comparison with experimental data in Figure 1H, I.

claim: A change of input of 25% leads to a change of 20±1% in membrane depolarization, averaged over all conditions.
source: Averaged over all conditions, a change of input of 25% lead to a change of 20±1% in membrane depolarization.
evidence: The claim is supported by averaging simulation results across different conditions.

claim: There is a nearly linear relationship between the activated number of synapses and the measured amplitude in the soma regardless of synaptic strength.
source: Our simulations revealed a nearly linear relationship between the activated number of synapses and the measured amplitude in the soma regardless of synaptic strength (Figure 5I).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Processing of odor information in the MB largely depends on the stochastic connectivity of projection neurons to KCs.
source: In contrast to most axon guidance processes in Drosophila that are essentially identical in all wild-type individuals, processing of odor information in the MB largely, but not exclusively, depends on the stochastic connectivity of projection neurons to KCs that relay odor information from the olfactory glomeruli to the MBONs (Caron et al., 2013; Gruntman and Turner, 2013; Litwin-Kumar et al., 2017; Warth Pérez Arias et al., 2020; Zheng et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The role of MBONs within the circuit is largely fixed between animals.
source: However, the role of MBONs within the circuit is largely fixed between animals and many MBONs can be classified as either approach or avoidance neurons in specific behavioral paradigms (Aso et al., 2014a; Aso et al., 2014b; Litwin-Kumar et al., 2017; Li et al., 2020; Takemura et al., 2017; Scheffer et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Individual KCs are not biased in their MBON connectivity but innervate both approach and avoidance output modules.
source: Furthermore, individual KCs are not biased in their MBON connectivity but innervate both kinds of output modules, for both approach and avoidance.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about KC connectivity patterns.

claim: Learning and memory is incorporated via the local activity of valence-encoding DANs that can either depress or potentiate KC>MBON synaptic connections.
source: Learning and memory, the modulation of odor response behavior through pairing of an individual odor with either positive or negative valence, is incorporated via the local activity of valence-encoding DANs that can either depress or potentiate KC>MBON synaptic connections (Aso and Rubin, 2016; Berry et al., 2018; Handler et al., 2019; Yamagata et al., 2015; Cohn et al., 2015; Burke et al., 2012; Hige et al., 2015a; Owald et al., 2015a; Jacob and Waddell, 2020; Pai et al., 2013; Plaçais et al., 2013; Séjourné et al., 2011; Bouzaiane et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The dendritic tree of the MBON is electrotonically compact, despite the complex architecture that includes a high degree of branching.
source: Our data show that the dendritic tree of the MBON is electrotonically compact, despite the complex architecture that includes a high degree of branching.
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results showing voltage compactification.

claim: Electrotonic compactness in MBON-α3 is in agreement with prior electrophysiological characterization of an MBON in locust.
source: This data is in agreement with a prior electrophysiological characterization of an MBON in locust (Cassenaer and Laurent, 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with cited literature.

claim: Electrotonic compactness supports linear integration of synaptic inputs across extensive arborizations and likely serves to functionally compensate for inter-individual variability.
source: and a similar feature has been reported for neurons in the stomatogastric ganglion of crayfish. Here the electrotonic compactness supports linear integration of synaptic inputs across extensive arborizations and likely serves to functionally compensate for inter-individual variability (Otopalik et al., 2017; Otopalik et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies in crayfish neurons.

claim: The location of an individual synaptic input within the dendritic tree has only a minor effect on the amplitude of the neuron's output, despite large variations of local dendritic potentials.
source: The location of an individual synaptic input within the dendritic tree has therefore only a minor effect on the amplitude of the neuron's output, despite large variations of local dendritic potentials.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from simulation results showing voltage compactification.

claim: In contrast to large vertebrate neurons, local active amplification or other compensatory mechanisms may not be necessary to support input normalization in the dendritic tree of small central neurons in Drosophila.
source: Together with the relatively small size of many central neurons in Drosophila, this indicates that in contrast to large vertebrate neurons, local active amplification or other compensatory mechanisms (Rumsey and Abbott, 2006; Sterratt et al., 2012; Froemke et al., 2005; Gidon and Segev, 2009; Schiller et al., 2000; Polsky et al., 2004) may not be necessary to support input normalization in the dendritic tree.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the compactness results and comparison with vertebrate neurons.

claim: Voltage-gated Na+ channels are localized in putative spike initiation zones in a subset of central neurons of Drosophila.
source: In contrast, for axons it has been recently reported that voltage-gated Na+ channels are localized in putative spike initiation zones in a subset of central neurons of Drosophila (Ravenscroft et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ravenscroft et al., 2020.

claim: Individual odors evoke activity reliably in approximately 3–9% of KCs based on calcium imaging in vivo.
source: Calcium imaging in vivo demonstrated that individual odors evoke activity reliably in approximately 3–9% of KCs (Campbell et al., 2013; Honegger et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to calcium imaging studies.

claim: Simulations of 1000 independent trials with random sets of 50 KCs demonstrate that such activation patterns robustly elicit MBON activity in agreement with in vivo observations.
source: Our simulations of 1000 independent trials with random sets of 50 KCs, each representing one distinct odor that activates approximately 5% of the KCs innervating the target MBON, demonstrate that such activation patterns robustly elicit MBON activity in agreement with in vivo observations of odor-induced activity that elicited robust increases in action potential frequency in MBONs (Hige et al., 2015a; Warth Pérez Arias et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results and comparison with cited in vivo observations.

claim: The low variability of depolarizations observed in simulations indicates that information coding by activation patterns is highly robust.
source: The low variability of depolarizations observed in these simulations indicates that information coding by such activation patterns is highly robust.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from simulation results.

claim: Labeled line representations of odor identity are likely not necessary at the level of KCs since relaying information via any set of ≈50 KCs is of approximately equal efficiency.
source: As a consequence, labeled line representations of odor identity are likely not necessary at the level of KCs since relaying information via any set of ≈50 KCs is of approximately equal efficiency.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from simulation results showing robust and consistent activation.

claim: Variability in parameters controlling neuronal excitability of individual KCs negatively affects associative memory performance.
source: Such a model is supported by a recent computational study demonstrating that variability in parameters controlling neuronal excitability of individual KCs negatively affects associative memory performance.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a computational study.

claim: Compensatory variation mechanisms exist that ensure similar activity levels between all odor-encoding KC sets to maintain efficient memory performance.
source: The authors provide evidence that compensatory variation mechanisms exist that ensure similar activity levels between all odor-encoding KC sets to maintain efficient memory performance (Abdelrahman et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Abdelrahman et al., 2021.

claim: Optical recordings of in vivo activity of MBONs revealed selective reductions in MBON activity in response to aversive odor training.
source: Optical recordings of in vivo activity of MBONs revealed selective reductions in MBON activity in response to aversive odor training (Jacob and Waddell, 2020; Pai et al., 2013; Owald and Waddell, 2015; Perisse et al., 2016; Séjourné et al., 2011) or to optogenetic activation of selective DANs (Hige et al., 2015a).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to optical recording studies.

claim: Both depression and potentiation of MBON activity have been previously observed in different MBON modules in vivo.
source: More generally, both depression and potentiation of MBON activity have been previously observed in different MBON modules in vivo (Owald and Waddell, 2015; Hige et al., 2015a; Perisse et al., 2016; Plaçais et al., 2013; Pai et al., 2013; Séjourné et al., 2011; Jacob and Waddell, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to in vivo studies.

claim: Recent studies have observed changes in KC stimulus representations after conditioning.
source: In addition, recent studies have observed changes in KC stimulus representations after conditioning (Delestro et al., 2020; Shyu et al., 2019) that may be due to learning-dependent modulations of synaptic PN input to KCs (Baltruschat et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Changes in KC stimulus representations after conditioning may be due to learning-dependent modulations of synaptic PN input to KCs.
source: In addition, recent studies have observed changes in KC stimulus representations after conditioning (Delestro et al., 2020; Shyu et al., 2019) that may be due to learning-dependent modulations of synaptic PN input to KCs (Baltruschat et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on cited studies.

claim: The two different mechanisms of altering MBON output (synaptic strength vs. KC number) are potentially utilized for the establishment of different types of memory.
source: The two different mechanisms of altering MBON output are potentially utilized for the establishment of different types of memory with fast and local alterations of synaptic transmission likely essential for short-term memory while structural changes may ensure maintenance of memory over long periods of time.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from simulation results.

claim: Fast and local alterations of synaptic transmission are likely essential for short-term memory.
source: The two different mechanisms of altering MBON output are potentially utilized for the establishment of different types of memory with fast and local alterations of synaptic transmission likely essential for short-term memory while structural changes may ensure maintenance of memory over long periods of time.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference.

claim: Structural changes may ensure maintenance of memory over long periods of time.
source: The two different mechanisms of altering MBON output are potentially utilized for the establishment of different types of memory with fast and local alterations of synaptic transmission likely essential for short-term memory while structural changes may ensure maintenance of memory over long periods of time.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference.

claim: The KC>MBON architecture represents a biophysical module that is well-suited to simultaneously process changes based on either synaptic and/or network modulation.
source: Our simulation data thus shows that the KC>MBON architecture represents a biophysical module that is well-suited to simultaneously process changes based on either synaptic and/or network modulation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from simulation results.

claim: The interplay between KCs and MBONs ensures reliable information processing and memory storage despite the stochastic connectivity of the memory circuitry.
source: Together with the electrotonic nature of the MBONs, the interplay between KCs and MBONs thus ensures reliable information processing and memory storage despite the stochastic connectivity of the memory circuitry.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the overall study results.

claim: MBON-α3 can be accessed genetically by using a specific Gal4 line (MB082C-Gal4).
source: In addition, we can access MBON-α3 genetically by using a specific Gal4 line (MB082C-Gal4) to label MBON-α3 by the expression of membrane-bound GFP (10xUAS-IVS-mCD8::GFP; Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental methodology and Figure 1A.

claim: The MB082C-Gal4 line marks two different MBON-α3 cells that are almost identical with regard to their dendritic tree position and synaptic input number.
source: It is of note that we cannot discriminate between the two different MBON-α3 cells that are marked by the split Gal4 line and that are almost identical with regard to their dendritic tree position and synaptic input number (Takemura et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Takemura et al., 2017.

claim: Kenyon cells are cholinergic.
source: As KCs are cholinergic (Barnstedt et al., 2016) we utilized previously determined parameters of cholinergic synapses to simulate synaptic input to MBON-α3.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Barnstedt et al., 2016.

claim: The faster voltage change at the onset and offset of the current injection seen in the simulation is caused by the small size of the soma which results in a much faster 'local' somatic time constant than that of the whole cell.
source: Note that the faster voltage change at the onset and offset of the current injection seen in the simulation is caused by the small size of the soma which results in a much faster 'local' somatic time constant than that of the whole cell (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the cell morphology and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: More distal dendritic segments (more distant from the soma) have a smaller volume and diameter.
source: Representing the distance between dendritic inputs and soma (Figure 3G) by a color code, we find that, as in many tree-like structures, there is a systematic tendency that more distal segments (more distant from the soma) have a smaller volume and diameter, Figure 3H.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 3G and 3H.

claim: Placing an electrical charge (integrated synaptic current) on a small capacitor (low-volume segment with small surface area) results in a larger voltage excursion than placing the same charge on a large capacitor (large segment).
source: This is expected: placing an electrical charge (integrated synaptic current) on a small capacitor (low-volume segment with small surface area) results in a larger voltage excursion than placing the same charge on a large capacitor (large segment).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of electrical circuits.
